heroLead: Eau Claire sits in northern Butler County, small-town ground where shallow gas wells older than most living memory still quietly produce alongside newer Marcellus development.
intro: Northern Butler County has a shallow gas history that goes back over a century, and Eau Claire-area families often hold a mineral interest tied to that legacy production without fully knowing its current status. It's common for us to hear from an owner who's been receiving a small, steady royalty check for years and has no idea whether the well behind it is even still actively maintained, or whether there's a separate, deeper Marcellus lease on the same land they've never been told about.
We're glad to look at whatever paperwork or statements you have and sort out exactly what your family's interest covers before making a cash offer.

sections.heading: A Legacy of Shallow Wells in Northern Butler County
paragraphs: Thousands of shallow gas wells were drilled across Butler County in the early 1900s, and a meaningful number of them are still technically producing today, decades past what anyone might expect from a well that old. Eau Claire-area leases from this era often use simple one-eighth royalty language that predates modern deduction practices and horizontal drilling entirely.
If your family's interest traces back to one of these old wells, we look at the well's actual current production before discussing what a lump-sum offer might reasonably reflect.

sections.heading: Whether Deep Rights Were Ever Addressed
paragraphs: A common question we run into near Eau Claire is whether an old shallow-well lease also covers the deeper Marcellus interval, or whether that depth was never addressed and remains open. The answer depends entirely on the specific lease language, which varies well by well in this part of Butler County. We review the actual document rather than assuming either way.

sections.heading: Deciding Whether a Small Check Is Worth Keeping
paragraphs: A small, steady royalty check from a legacy well can feel like it's not worth the trouble of selling, but it also isn't necessarily worth much to hold onto for another twenty years if the well is deep into its decline. We'll look honestly at the production trend and tell you whether a cash offer now makes more sense than continuing to wait on shrinking quarterly payments.
